reason: The Court held that post-1977 hypothecary defaults fall under the general CPC provisions and that non-service makes the judgment a nullity capable of being set aside.
The case turned on the specific Partition Law section 48(4) category for an unrepresented claimant, not a general distinction between lawyer-made and personal claims.
The Court applied the rule that, where a genuine partition settlement exists, the court need only be satisfied that all interested parties are included, while finding this petitioner was not bound.
The Court held that a tenant-cultivator lease granted pendente lite in breach of section 67 of the Partition Act was void.
The Court construed Regulation 8 as giving the Corporation a discretion to issue a gemming licence on satisfaction of consent from owners of more than two-thirds of co-owned land.
The Court held that a partition scheme must provide access to a public right of way from within the corpus rather than by imposing access over outside land.
The statement omits the material requirement that the parties must agree on the premises, tenancy period, and rent payable.
The Court treated proof of rent payment, especially rent receipts, as the best test for establishing tenancy in the delivery-of-possession dispute.
The statement is too vague and omits the two determinations required under Partition Law sections 52(2), 48(1), and Rent Act section 14(1).
The holding was about a Rent Act six-month notice for a monthly tenancy in a leap year, not an unqualified rule about every notice to vacate.
The Court held that the Rent Act notice was bad in law because the statutory six-month notice requirement was not complied with.
The Court held that non-compliance with the statutory six-month written notice prejudiced the tenant by depriving him of a statutory right.
The bill-of-lading date was a factual step in assessing the amended credit condition, not a legal rule decided by the Court.
The statement omits the decisive facts that the letter-of-credit condition was added after shipment and was impossible for the supplier to fulfil.
The Court applied the injunction principle that where the alleged loss is quantified in damages, the balance of convenience generally weighs against injunctive relief.
The statement overgeneralizes a partition-sale purchaser's obligation to deposit sale proceeds for the beneficiary into a rule about any party.
The extracted quote is truncated and the statement omits that section 47 was inapplicable only because the case did not involve several-party distribution claims.
The Court held that the Civil Procedure Code joinder provisions are procedural, not substantive, and should be applied with a common-sense approach.
The quote is truncated and the statement omits that section 18 permits striking out an improperly joined party on application before the hearing.
The Court held that an action instituted against a deceased sole defendant is coram non judice and the resulting judgment is void.
The Court held that a person affected by void proceedings may seek to set them aside ex debito justitiae under the court's inherent jurisdiction.
The Court held that an urban-tenement tenancy depends on the continued existence of the building and cannot subsist over bare land after demolition.
The Court applied the principle that a monthly tenant's protected rights are not extinguished merely by a partition decree under section 48.
The Court construed section 121(2) as requiring witness and document lists to be filed fifteen days before the trial date after notice to the opposite party.
The statement omits the material circumstances of late filing, no explanation, prejudice to the plaintiff, and the plaintiff having already closed his case.
